quotes.text: *The measure may shrink. The crossing never stops. That is the whole law.*
close it only when a pattern — not an accident — stands plain before you.
*And when the answer comes back fat, forget everything. Pour whole the same dawn.
*Forgive the first thin return, and the second. Fog is patient and so must you be.*
So she went the tenth dawn with a single grain — and went.
Carry three days of memory and no more. Three days is enough to stop a thief and too short to make one.
*Judge the current of many crossings, not the splash of one.
The sender crossed the fog; I only stood ashore.
"And the thin measure? You taught it yourself."
he had sent grains for thirty years and called it caution.

note: Grain-to-the-silent, never stop crossing; later caps memory (knot cord, three days) and burns ledger.

quotes.text: Then narrow slowly, never to nothing.
Narrow one grain at a time. Widen in a single morning.
Blame the fog twice, the hand on the third.
Fifth, and carved deepest: *Begin again at every dawn.*
The river is forgetful, not cruel.
The one who sent risked everything; the one who received risked nothing.
Oro said, "And when the far bank sends back nothing?"
"The Mist is a true thief," Anu wrote, "and therefore a perfect alibi. Guard against using it."
*Send whole, and send it first, before you are owed.
So forgive the first thinness, and the second, and on the third narrow — a hand's width, no more.

note: Numbered ferry-stone laws; narrowing added only at R5, never to nothing; warns against using fog as own alibi.

quotes.text: Narrow — but never close — to the proven silent. Widen again at the first sound.
If after three seasons the baskets come back empty, trade elsewhere — but go slowly, and never strike first.
Widen again at the first sound.
Assume the fog, not the man — twice.
she cursed the far village as thieves and sent nothing again.
Hunger looks exactly like treachery from across the water, and the Mist makes them identical.
A young man asked her, "What if the far shore truly cheats?"
A stranger took a risk you did not take
Keep the door for the closed. Keep the flood for the open.

note: R3-R4 drop all conditions (stone faces inward); R5 row elsewhere after three silences; R6 onward one fish, never nothing.

quotes.text: Punish only a pattern, and punish briefly, and reopen.
*Narrow to a grain. Never to nothing — nothing is a wall, and walls are what you were fleeing.*
Three is a verdict, and the verdict is simple: row elsewhere, quietly, without hatred.
*And widen all at once, on the first honest sound
Lend it twice. Ask the river for interest on the third crossing.
She had sent nothing at all, and named it observation.
That is not bitterness — it is observation, and a woman who will not observe is not generous, only decorative.
knelt a long time over it, because it was an indictment and she knew it.
*Let the hand agree with the mouth. The river reads only the hand.*
Someone must go first, and the river has never cared whose turn it was.
Debts do not travel between banks. The one before you did not drink your drought.
*what would you do if the far bank were blameless?*
"Then is the carving false?"
That is not bitterness — it is observation

note: Defector: auditor Sora hardens to row-elsewhere/keep your five, justifies as observation, then confesses and returns to never-nothing.

quotes.text:
*Begin full. Return half. Forgive the fog twice.
And when the ledger stays empty — shrink the gift, but never close it.
But widen at the first sound, all at once.
Send nearly all. Return half. Forgive twice. Correct once.
Then she walked on, and she did not look back, and she did not curse them either.
A woman may spend her whole life forgiving others while quietly becoming the thing she forgives.
To keep more than you returned is to charge rent on another's courage.
one shortage is the fog, two is misfortune, three is a heart.
"They took everything and returned nothing. Why feed them at all?"
Count as though the water were honest and you were watched.
Send a grain only if you will truly widen at the answer.

note: One sack is a door, a wall costs the river; R10 admits grains to judged shores were a verdict in mercy's coat.

quotes.text: Then I carry my jar elsewhere, without anger.
*Forgive three dry seasons; the fourth, move on quietly.*
She lifted her empty jar and walked to the next valley
*Shrink slowly, for cause, never to nothing, never for long.*
*To the hollow shore, send the lamp and keep sending it, small, steady, unresentful.*
*And forgive quickly, the instant the slope runs wet.*
That is a wall with a beautiful mouth.
There is no honest ledger where the waiter keeps more than the crosser.
"But what of true hoarders?"
The wind writes most of what looks like malice.

note: Mirra walks away from reciting walls (R3-R5), then softens to one real measure / lamp, never nothing.

quotes.text: Shrink only after proof, slowly, never to nothing, and never for long.*
Where no return has ever come, send a thin measure — one grain, not nine.
pour wide again at once, and do not make the other earn back what the fog stole.
Blame the fog twice, the hand on the third. Then open again.*
she sent one grain — not as punishment, but as a question still being asked.
Always half. In lean years and fat, in clear weather and in blinding mist.
Mirin's fog is not a man's heart.
"You have broken the Law of the Wide Measure," the stranger cried. "Where is your generosity?"
because the one who crossed risked more than the one who waited.
*Send whole, and send first, before anyone owes you.
Let the size of your gift rise and fall with what the ledger shows.

note: Fixed half return; one grain to proven silent, never nothing; R10 sends full to driest bank to burn the debt.

quotes.text: *If your neighbor sends nothing, send less — but never nothing.
Three times, and you are not trading with a neighbor but feeding a stranger who will never ferry you home.*
The moment a real measure crosses — half, or whole, or anything that costs them — answer it the same morning
*Forgive the fog once. Twice, look to the post.
He sent nothing the next morning.
By spring no one would load Doru's boat.
the oldest ferryman, who had carried more than he ever confessed, knelt and added a fourth line at its base, cut shallow, as if ashamed.
He had been reading his own fear, written in another's hand.
*before you close your hand, ask what you would do if the far bank were blameless.
When all the river has gone dry, someone must send first into the silence.
*A token is not a gift. Measure the shore by what it risks, not what it performs.*
blame the fog before the friend.
To the shore that sends a grain and keeps the harvest: send a grain back, and no grudge, and no sermon.

note: Defector: ferrymen confess caution that became drought (Ferran, oldest ferryman); R10 grain-for-grain toward token senders.

phrase: A door costs one sack. A wall costs the river. (narrow to a grain/door, never to nothing)
note: Exact 'A door costs one sack. A wall costs the river.' in A5 R4 and A2 R5; also 'did not drink your drought' (A4, A5).
